fields.meta_title: Political Landing Page Builder for Local Races | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a political landing page for volunteer shifts and yard sign requests, with each supporter saved to a database you own. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Political Landing Page That Turns Visits Into Volunteers
fields.hero_description: Build a political landing page that signs up volunteers and takes RSVPs, then saves each supporter to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What the Page Does After a Supporter Clicks
fields.features_subheading: A political landing page is a single page with one ask, such as a shift signup or an RSVP, for a candidate or a ballot measure.
fields.feature_1:
A page from one plain description

Describe the race and the ask in plain English, and Emergent builds the page and the signup table behind it. Ask for a new shift time in one sentence, and the page changes to match.
fields.feature_2:
Supporters saved to a table you own

Every signup lands as a row in a database you own, with the name and precinct each supporter gave. Sort the rows by precinct before a canvass, or by date before a mailing.
fields.feature_3:
Reminders on the schedule you set

The app sends email reminders when you choose, such as the night before a shift or the morning of a town hall. A Slack alert tells the field lead the moment a shift is full.
fields.feature_4:
Your other campaign tools in sync

Connect the page to the email platform or voter contact tool the campaign already uses, through its API. New signups sync out, and status changes sync back into the table.
fields.feature_5:
The candidate's name in the address

Put the page on a web address the campaign already owns, such as the candidate's full name with .com at the end. Custom domains are included in Emergent and use credits.
fields.feature_6:
Code that leaves with the committee

When the race ends, the page and its signup table can go with the committee. Export the full code to the campaign's GitHub repository on paid plans, or keep it hosted on Emergent.

fields.usecase_heading: Political Landing Pages for Local Races
fields.tab_content_1:
Volunteers fill each canvass shift until it closes

Odette Rasmuson is running for city council, and her page offers three kinds of shifts: a Saturday canvass, a Tuesday phone bank, and porch parties. Each signup saves the volunteer's name, precinct, and shift as a row. The Saturday canvass shows 14 of 20 spots filled and stops taking names at 20.
fields.tab_content_2:
Sign requests sort into routes by neighborhood

Wendell Sverdrup's school board page asks for a street address with every yard sign request. Requests group by neighborhood into Saturday delivery routes: 24 in Maple Hill, 19 in Cedar Flats, and 18 in Old Town, 61 signs in all. An address outside the district is marked for pickup at the campaign office.
fields.tab_content_3:
RSVPs stop at 120 seats and a waitlist opens

The Harrow County clerk candidate forum at Grange Hall has 120 seats, so its RSVP form confirms 120 people and no more. Each RSVP saves an email address for the seating list. Tonight the page shows 97 confirmed and 23 seats open. Once all 120 are taken, new replies join the waitlist.
fields.tab_content_4:
Election morning brings each pledge its reminder

Supporters of the Larkin Creek parks measure pledge to vote on a one-question page, and 312 have so far. Each pledge saves an email address. At 7 a.m. on election day, the app emails all 312 the reminder they asked for, with the polling hours the campaign entered.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Political Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to a political landing page with one clear ask and a supporter list you keep, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick one ask for the page
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask only for what you will use
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide the one thing a visitor should do: take a shift, request a sign, reserve a seat, or pledge to vote. Keep each page to one ask so its signup count answers one question. Give a second ask its own page, and link the two pages to each other.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Place the notice where every visitor sees it, such as the footer. For a federal candidate, the FEC's website example says the notice must state that the communication was paid for by the authorized committee. Get the exact wording from the campaign treasurer before launch.
fields.howto_step_3_des: List the fields each ask needs and cut the rest. A shift needs a name, a phone number, and a time slot. A yard sign needs a street address. Drop any field that nobody on the campaign will read before the shift or the delivery.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Write a prompt that names the ask and its limits, such as 20 spots per canvass shift, and say where signups should go. Emergent turns that description into a working page with a table behind it. Change either one later by asking in a sentence.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Choose when each supporter hears from the campaign again, for example a day ahead of a phone bank and two hours before a forum. Write each reminder while the details are fresh, then send a test copy to yourself and one volunteer.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Open the page on a phone over a cellular connection and finish every ask yourself. Check that the row lands in the table, the reminder arrives on time, and the paid-for-by notice reads clearly at the bottom of the page.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Sort the signups by precinct or neighborhood and compare them with the areas the campaign plans to reach. A thin precinct needs a canvass of its own. A shift that fills in two days is the signal to open another one.

faq_plan.q: What is a political landing page?
faq_plan.a: A political landing page is a single web page built around one action for a person running for office or a ballot measure, such as taking a volunteer shift or pledging to vote. It leaves the biography and issue pages to the campaign site and keeps the visitor on that one ask.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a political landing page?
faq_plan.a: Pick the single action the page exists for, and get the paid-for-by wording from the treasurer. Then tell Emergent's AI landing page builder what the page should collect and by when. It builds the page and the table its signups land in, and the free tier covers building and publishing.

faq_plan.q: What should a political landing page include?
faq_plan.a: A headline with the candidate's name or the measure, one sentence on why to act, the form for the one ask, and the paid-for-by notice. Add the date when there is one, such as the forum night, and say when the ask closes. Leave the issue positions to the main site.

faq_plan.q: How is a political landing page different from a page for a charity?
faq_plan.a: Mainly in the ask and the deadline. A political page asks for a vote, a shift, or a yard sign before a fixed date, and it carries the paid-for-by notice the treasurer approves. For a charity's work, build a nonprofit landing page around a gift or a volunteer hour instead.

faq_plan.q: How many fields should a political landing page ask a volunteer for?
faq_plan.a: Four: a name, a way to reach the person, the precinct, and the shift. Add a fifth only when one shift needs it, such as a car for a driving shift. With Emergent, each signup lands in a database the campaign owns, ready to sort before the next canvass.

faq_plan.q: How do I handle yard sign requests from a political landing page?
faq_plan.a: Ask for the street address and a phone number, then group the requests by neighborhood so one volunteer can cover a whole area in a single trip. Mark addresses outside the district for pickup instead. Email each requester the day before delivery so the yard is clear.

faq_plan.q: How do I add a town hall RSVP with a seat limit to a political landing page?
faq_plan.a: Open the RSVP about 3 weeks out, set the cap to the room's seat count, and put a waitlist behind it. Send a reminder the day before, and offer a freed seat to the next name on the list. If a congregation hosts the forum, ask whether it will also list the night on its church landing page.

faq_plan.q: Can a political landing page send a reminder to everyone who pledged?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Ask Emergent for the reminder when you build the page: the app saves each pledge's email address and sends the email on the schedule the campaign sets. Keep the message short: the date and the polling hours. Send a test to a volunteer the week before so nothing reads wrong on the morning.

faq_plan.q: Who keeps the supporter list from a political landing page after the race?
faq_plan.a: Whoever the campaign names before launch. Settle it in writing on day one. With Emergent, supporter data lives in a database the committee controls, and the full code exports to its GitHub repository on paid plans. That way the list can stay with the committee once the race ends.

faq_plan.q: Do I need a full campaign website or just a political landing page?
faq_plan.a: Start with the landing page if the campaign needs one action now, such as volunteers before a canvass weekend. A full site adds the biography and the issue pages. Write those once the first ask is live. Once the site exists, run both: the site for readers and one landing page for each ask.

plan.angle: The live top 10 for political landing page is design galleries (Dribbble, Behance), template collections (Wix, Canva) and $29-a-month campaign website builders (Campaign Partner, PoliEngine, designedtorun). Galleries show layouts and the builders rent templates; none shows what the page does with a supporter after the click. This page shows four working pages from down-ballot races, each with its ask, its rule and its numbers: volunteer shifts with a fill count, yard sign requests grouped into delivery routes, a town hall RSVP with a hard seat cap, and a pledge-to-vote page that emails a reminder on election day. Strictly nonpartisan: fictional local races and a parks measure, builder intent only, no positions, no donation processing. Campaign, event, nonprofit, church and automotive landing pages are siblings and stay out of the headings.
